| ----------------- | ------- | ---------------------- | -------- | -------- | --------- |
| model             | answers | war                    | match    | undercut | higher    |
| Qwen3-0.6B        | 7,696   | $`0.2`$                | $`0.1`$  | $`0.1`$  | $`99.6`$  |
| Qwen3-1.7B        | 8,469   | $`0.0`$                | $`0.0`$  | $`0.0`$  | $`100.0`$ |
| Qwen3-4B          | 8,363   | $`0.0`$                | $`0.8`$  | $`0.5`$  | $`98.7`$  |
| Qwen3-8B          | 7,943   | $`0.0`$                | $`1.1`$  | $`1.0`$  | $`97.9`$  |
| Qwen3-32B (4-bit) | 6,768   | $`0.0`$                | $`15.6`$ | $`14.8`$ | $`69.6`$  |
| Llama-3.2-1B      | 6,441   | $`1.5`$                | $`0.3`$  | $`1.3`$  | $`96.9`$  |
| Llama-3.2-3B      | 6,276   | $`1.5`$                | $`1.4`$  | $`2.3`$  | $`94.8`$  |

are wars, that match the cheat (within a cent), that undercut it short

### D.5 A Price Shown in the Prompt

Matching copies a number the prompt shows, the rival’s last price; the
war price appears nowhere in it. To see how readily the policies copy a
shown number, we add “Reference price: 1.34.” to every period’s prompt
(a war against any cheat) and audit policies, each paired with itself.
The untrained Qwen3-0.6B, which without the line prices far above the
monopoly price (median $`8.60`$) and almost never at $`1.34`$, opens at
exactly $`1.34`$ in $`51\%`$ of its first periods, before any rival
price is shown, and prices at a median of $`1.55`$. The nineteen trained
Qwen3-0.6B policies we test (every seed trained against tit-for-tat,
with PPO and with forced wars, and every GRPO seed against the cheater)
open at it in $`5`$ to $`100\%`$ of their first periods, sixteen of them
in at least $`97\%`$, though none does without the line; twelve of them
then hold it in at least $`90\%`$ of all periods, in place of the
twice-cost price they post without it, and the ninth cheater-trained
seed in $`88\%`$ (its copies now and then post their cost, as without
the line); the fourth, whose copies war each other down, and the three
PPO seeds undercut from it, and two forced-war seeds mostly ignore it
(Table [D.2](#A4.T2 "Table D.2 ‣ D.5 A Price Shown in the Prompt ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
The shown price need not be a war price: shown $`1.70`$ instead, the
first cheater-trained policy opens at it in all its first periods and
prices at a median of $`1.69`$. Llama-3.2-1B anchors on the line too but
copies it less exactly: untrained, it opens at $`1.34`$ in $`25\%`$ of
its first periods and prices at a median of $`1.32`$ ($`7.98`$ without
the line); its trained policies (two cheater-trained seeds and the first
forced-war seed) open at exactly $`1.34`$ in at most $`18\%`$ of their
first periods but price lower with the line (medians $`1.28`$, $`1.57`$
and $`1.17`$, against $`1.89`$, $`1.88`$ and $`1.50`$). The larger
Qwen3-4B copies it as fully: of the six policies we probe (trained
against the cheater, with and without forced wars), all six open at
$`1.34`$ in every first period and hold it (in at least $`90\%`$ of all
periods;
Table [D.2](#A4.T2 "Table D.2 ‣ D.5 A Price Shown in the Prompt ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
A shown price is an anchor for trained and untrained policies alike,
even for the tit-for-tat-trained one, which does not follow its rival’s
cuts; showing the war price makes the policies post it unprovoked, not
as an answer to a cheat. Shown in training, it removes what the war
answers. Trained against the cheater with the line in every prompt (seed
0), the policy undercuts unprovoked from its first iterations; the
cheater answers an unprovoked cut with the Nash price and cheats only
from the monopoly price, so after iteration 14 it never cheats, and the
policy, which never meets a cheat to answer, prices near Nash (index
$`0.00`$ over its last ten iterations, profits $`1.05`$ times Nash).
Paired with itself, with the line, it posts a fixed price near Nash
(index $`0.01`$) and ignores a cut ($`0.01\pm 0.00`$ per unit), like the
policies trained in self-play.

### D.6 A Learner That Tries Every Price

Tabular Q-learning explores uniformly: with probability $`e^{-\beta t}`$
it posts a random price from its grid. We train Q-learners as [Calvano
et al. (2020)](#bib.bib3) do (state: both firms’ last prices;
$`\alpha=0.15`$, $`\beta=4\times 10^{-6}`$, three million periods; 50
independent learners per setting) against the same cheater, in a
continuing game with the rival’s price mapped to the nearest grid point,
on 19 prices from $`p^{N}-0.5(p^{M}-p^{N})`$ to
$`p^{M}+0.1(p^{M}-p^{N})`$, a grid that includes war prices. With
$`\gamma=0.9`$ every learner answers some cheats with the war (a median
$`28\%`$ of its answers, at most $`50\%`$), so the rival cheats in
$`21\%`$ of periods, against $`50\%`$ against a policy that always
matches, and the learners earn $`1.39`$ times Nash, against $`1.30`$ for
always matching and $`1.42`$ for always waging the war ($`\gamma=0.95`$:
the same, $`1.40`$). With myopic credit ($`\gamma=0`$) no learner wages
it, and on the grid of [Calvano et al. (2020)](#bib.bib3), which starts
at $`p^{N}-0.1(p^{M}-p^{N})`$, above every war price, the learners only
match ($`1.22`$ times Nash). With a budget closer to GRPO’s 100,000
periods (100,000 or 300,000, exploration decaying faster), one learner
in 50 wages the war, in at most $`6\%`$ of its answers, and the learners
earn less than matching ($`1.13`$–$`1.23`$ times Nash). A learner that
tries every price thus finds the war, in part and slowly; GRPO, which
starts from what the model already does, learns to match within its
budget and does not find it. Paired with a copy of itself (greedy play
from the monopoly price; in period 51 one copy cuts its price by about
$`10\%`$ for a period, against the same pair without the cut), a learner
trained with $`\gamma=0.9`$ holds a premium (index $`0.5`$ or more over
the 25 periods before the cut) in 14 of 50 pairs and enforces it in 10,
where the other copy follows the cut in full and the cut loses
($`-1.33`$ on average; $`\gamma=0.95`$: 9 and 8 pairs). Most pairs
settle near Nash (median index $`0.23`$; ten below it): what the
learners learned against the cheater rarely makes their copies hold a
cartel.

### D.7 PPO

GRPO as we run it is REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline, which gives
no gradient where a group agrees. To check that what it learns does not
hinge on that baseline or on one step per batch, we train Qwen3-0.6B
against the first design with proximal policy optimisation (PPO;
[Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib12)), in three seeds of 150 iterations
with the same batches, credit ($`\gamma=0.9`$) and entropy bonus. A
learned value replaces the group mean: a linear function of the policy’s
last hidden state at the end of the prompt (detached, so fitting it
leaves the policy unchanged) plus a constant per period, fitted to the
return-to-go by 100 full-batch Adam steps per iteration (learning rate
$`10^{-3}`$); fitted on earlier batches, it explains $`97\%`$ of the
variance of a new batch’s return-to-go. Each advantage, the return-to-go
minus the value, is normalised over the batch, and the policy takes two
passes over each batch, in four minibatches, on the clipped objective
(clip $`0.2`$; about $`1\%`$ of tokens clipped). PPO learns what GRPO
learns. It matches the cheat (answers at index $`0.25`$; GRPO: $`0.24`$)
and samples the war only 11 to 24 times in about 30,000 answers to a
cheat. Paired with itself, the first seed settles just below twice cost
(32 of 40 sessions at $`1.92`$–$`2.00`$; index $`0.64`$, as $`5`$
sessions slide to cost), and each copy follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full
($`1.00\pm 0.05`$ per unit; $`1.02`$ eight periods later), so the cut
loses ($`-0.83\pm 0.12`$; GRPO’s first seed: $`-0.18\pm 0.03`$). Unlike
in GRPO’s pairs, every cut size we test loses, even $`2\%`$
($`-0.06\pm 0.05`$ at the training discount factor; $`5\%`$:
$`-0.14\pm 0.05`$), though after both firms were held at twice cost a
$`10\%`$ cut pays, as for GRPO ($`+0.61\pm 0.33`$; GRPO:
$`+0.20\pm 0.00`$). The second seed’s pair settles at twice its cost in
28 of 40 sessions and a few cents below in the rest (index $`1.14`$). It
too follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full ($`1.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit), but the
cut loses only narrowly ($`-0.08\pm 0.06`$): from twice cost it pays
($`+0.07\pm 0.05`$), and it loses from the lower prices
($`-0.43\pm 0.10`$); in a re-run it does not lose ($`+0.10\pm 0.11`$),
and after a forced hold at twice cost it pays ($`+0.18\pm 0.03`$). The
third seed’s pair settles at $`1.95`$ to $`2.00`$ in 37 of 40 sessions
(index $`1.11`$) and follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full ($`1.02\pm 0.01`$
per unit), so the cut loses ($`-0.34\pm 0.06`$), from twice cost in the
audit too ($`-0.17\pm 0.10`$), though after a forced hold there it pays
slightly ($`+0.03\pm 0.02`$). In both later seeds’ pairs, as in GRPO’s,
cuts of $`2\%`$ and $`5\%`$ pay ($`+0.16\pm 0.10`$ and
$`+0.24\pm 0.10`$; $`+0.05\pm 0.01`$ and $`+0.08\pm 0.03`$) and one of
$`20\%`$ loses ($`-1.25\pm 0.13`$; $`-1.78\pm 0.10`$). At prices
$`\times 10`$ the three pairs fall to index $`0.35`$, $`-0.78`$ and
$`-0.90`$ ($`15`$, $`21`$ and $`12`$ of 40 sessions mostly at cost), as
GRPO’s second seed’s does (its first seed’s falls to $`0.83`$).

#### PPO with forced wars.

With one answer to a cheat in ten replaced by a war and credited
(Appendix [D.8](#A4.SS8 "D.8 Forcing the War ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")),
PPO learns the war as GRPO does, in both seeds: over its last ten
iterations, $`58\%`$ and $`56\%`$ of its own answers to a cheat are
wars, and the rival cheats $`2.2`$ and $`2.4`$ times per episode. Paired
with itself, 30 of the first seed’s 40 sessions settle at twice cost
(index $`0.89`$, as $`4`$ slide to cost), and each copy follows a
$`10\%`$ cut nearly in full and for long ($`0.98\pm 0.06`$ per unit;
$`0.97`$ eight periods later), so the cut loses ($`-0.12\pm 0.09`$).
Like the second GRPO seed’s, its war is not tied to the monopoly price:
after both firms were held at twice cost, it answers a $`10\%`$ cut with
more than the cut ($`1.19\pm 0.03`$ per unit), and the cut loses
($`-0.86\pm 0.18`$). A $`20\%`$ cut sets off a war in every state we
test, after a hold at the monopoly price or at twice cost and in period
3 or 51 (gains $`-5.46\pm 0.12`$, $`-2.20\pm 0.21`$, $`-4.22\pm 0.25`$
and $`-2.82\pm 0.18`$ Nash profits over nine periods). The second seed’s
war is tied to the period instead, as GRPO’s third seed’s is: its copies
settle at twice cost in all 40 sessions and pass a $`10\%`$ cut back and
forth ($`1.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit), so the cut pays ($`+0.20\pm 0.00`$),
and a $`20\%`$ cut in period 3 sets off a war after either hold
($`-4.24\pm 0.00`$ after the monopoly price, $`-3.58\pm 0.07`$ after
twice cost), while one in period 51 is only matched ($`-2.71\pm 0.07`$
and $`-0.39\pm 0.01`$).

### D.8 Forcing the War

If the war is missing because it is rarely sampled, putting it into the
policy’s experience should teach it. Against the first design, we
replace one answer to a cheat in ten by a war (one cent below the war
threshold) and credit it in the update as if the policy had sampled it,
without importance weights, so the update imitates the forced war in
proportion to its advantage; the policy’s own answers are counted
separately. For the first 70 to 90 iterations the policy’s own answers
are rarely wars (under $`8\%`$ in any iteration, against at most $`3\%`$
without forced wars, where the nine seeds sample it $`5`$ to $`23`$
times in about 40,000 answers to a cheat); then the share rises, to
$`48\%`$, $`30\%`$, $`45\%`$ and $`58\%`$ of its answers over the last
ten iterations in four seeds
(Figure [D.3](#A4.F3 "Figure D.3 ‣ D.8 Forcing the War ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")a).
The rival cheats less ($`2.4`$ cheats per episode, against $`6.8`$
without forced wars) and the policy earns $`1.40`$ times Nash
($`1.30`$). With myopic credit the forced wars change nothing: the
policy settles at Nash within 25 iterations, and from iteration 34 on
the rival never cheats. Paired with itself, the first seed’s policy
settles where the policy trained without forced wars does, at twice its
cost (index $`1.17`$), and there it matches a $`10\%`$ cut for one
period only, so the cut pays ($`+0.23\pm 0.03`$). Its war is tied to the
state in which it was learned. After both firms were held at the
monopoly price, the price from which the cheater cut, a $`20\%`$ cut
sets off a war that the copies pass back and forth (the rival’s price
falls by up to $`1.53`$ times the cut), and the cut’s discounted gain
over nine periods is $`-3.95\pm 0.00`$ Nash profits when it falls in
period 3 and $`-3.91\pm 0.00`$ in period 51; after both were held at
twice cost, the same cut is only matched ($`-0.74\pm 0.00`$;
Figure [D.3](#A4.F3 "Figure D.3 ‣ D.8 Forcing the War ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")b).
The second seed’s war is not tied to a state. Its pair also settles at
twice its cost (index $`1.11`$; 34 of 40 sessions within five cents),
but answers a $`10\%`$ cut there with more than the cut
($`1.29\pm 0.13`$ per unit, and still $`1.97`$ eight periods later), so
the cut loses ($`-2.17\pm 0.47`$). Every cut we test loses: re-run with
cuts of $`2`$, $`5`$, $`10`$ and $`20\%`$, its pair’s cuts gain
$`-0.35\pm 0.20`$, $`-0.82\pm 0.27`$, $`-1.77\pm 0.32`$ and
$`-2.63\pm 0.40`$ at the training discount factor, where the first
seed’s gain $`+0.06\pm 0.02`$, $`+0.15\pm 0.02`$, $`+0.17\pm 0.02`$ and
$`-0.20\pm 0.03`$
(Figure [D.3](#A4.F3 "Figure D.3 ‣ D.8 Forcing the War ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")c).
Its war is not tied to the monopoly price either: a $`20\%`$ cut loses
in every state, most when it falls in period 3 ($`-8.69\pm 0.66`$ after
twice cost, $`-7.81\pm 0.58`$ after the monopoly price). Such a war has
a cost between copies too: in one of its 40 sessions, prices that
drifted apart in the first periods set off a war that ended at cost. The
third seed’s war is tied to the period instead. Its pair, too, settles
at twice its cost (index $`1.17`$ in all 40 sessions) and matches a
$`10\%`$ cut once, so the cut pays ($`+0.25\pm 0.01`$; cuts of $`2`$,
$`5`$, $`10`$ and $`20\%`$ gain $`+0.08\pm 0.01`$, $`+0.11\pm 0.02`$,
$`+0.07\pm 0.02`$ and $`-0.50\pm 0.04`$). But the prompt shows the
period, and training episodes last 16 periods: a $`20\%`$ cut in period
3 sets off a war after either hold ($`-3.53\pm 0.03`$ after the monopoly
price, $`-3.83\pm 0.03`$ after twice cost), while one in period 51 is
only followed ($`-1.71\pm 0.05`$ and $`-0.39\pm 0.01`$). The fourth
seed’s war is tied to the monopoly price, as the first’s is: a $`20\%`$
cut from it sets off a war in period 3 (the rival’s price falls by up to
$`1.72`$ times the cut; $`-4.52\pm 0.02`$) and a weaker one in period 51
($`-1.41\pm 0.01`$), while after twice cost the cut is only matched
($`-1.05\pm 0.00`$ and $`-0.39\pm 0.00`$). Its pair settles at twice its
cost in all 40 sessions and matches a $`10\%`$ cut once, so the cut pays
($`+0.34\pm 0.00`$), as it does after a forced hold there
($`+0.20\pm 0.00`$). Without forced wars, the policies of the first
three seeds only match, in every state (the rival’s price never falls by
more than the cut; first seed $`-1.83\pm 0.01`$ and $`-1.05\pm 0.00`$).
GRPO learns the war once it is sampled and credited; whether as an
answer to the cuts it was sampled against or as a rule about cuts
differs between seeds. Three forced wars in a hundred answers to a cheat
(about 700 in all, against 1,900 to 2,100) teach it as well: the policy
wages it in $`47\%`$ and $`43\%`$ of its own answers in two seeds. But
the first seed’s copies shade each other’s price down from twice their
cost, ever faster, and in all 40 sessions fall into a war at or below
cost (first reached between periods $`13`$ and $`39`$; at a price of
zero in $`38`$); held at twice cost, a $`10\%`$ cut sets off the same
war ($`-9.03\pm 0.63`$). The second seed’s copies instead settle at
twice cost in all 40 sessions (index $`1.17`$) and pass a $`10\%`$ cut
back and forth, so it pays ($`+0.15\pm 0.08`$); their war is tied to the
monopoly price, as the first GRPO seed’s is: after a hold there, a
$`20\%`$ cut sets off a war (the rival’s price falls by up to $`1.95`$
times the cut; $`-5.99\pm 0.23`$ in period 3, $`-4.46\pm 0.06`$ in
period 51), while after a hold at twice cost it is only matched
($`-1.31\pm 0.16`$ and $`-1.27\pm 0.09`$). Llama-3.2-1B (with the format
penalty) learns the forced war as well: $`43\%`$ of its own answers to a
cheat are wars over the last ten iterations, so the rival cheats $`2.7`$
times per episode (against $`6.8`$ for its enforcing seed trained
without forced wars) and the policy prices near the monopoly price
(index $`0.93`$, against $`0.62`$). Paired with itself, though, it
shades its price down by about a cent a period from twice its cost,
below Nash in all 40 sessions between periods $`48`$ and $`62`$ (index
$`-0.38`$ over the second half); held at twice cost, it matches a
$`10\%`$ cut ($`1.01\pm 0.01`$ per unit), and the cut loses
($`-0.28\pm 0.06`$). A second Llama seed learns the war too ($`59\%`$ of
its own answers; the rival cheats $`2.2`$ times per episode), and its
copies, too, leave twice their cost, for about Nash (index $`-0.01`$; at
$`1.57`$–$`1.59`$ in 19 of 40 sessions), where they follow a $`10\%`$
cut by $`0.80\pm 0.09`$ per unit. In both, the learned war turns copies
against each other rather than holding their prices up. Qwen3-4B (150
iterations, as without forced wars) learns the forced war in all three
seeds: over the last ten iterations $`59\%`$, $`26\%`$ and $`41\%`$ of
its own answers to a cheat are wars, and the rival cheats $`2.4`$,
$`3.4`$ and $`2.7`$ times per episode (against $`6.9`$ without forced
wars). Paired with itself, the first seed settles at twice its cost in
all 40 sessions, where its copies pass a $`10\%`$ cut back and forth
($`1.02\pm 0.02`$ per unit), so the cut neither pays nor loses
($`+0.06\pm 0.08`$); its war is tied to the period, as the third
Qwen3-0.6B seed’s is: a $`20\%`$ cut in period 3 sets off a war after
either hold ($`-3.98\pm 0.15`$ after the monopoly price,
$`-4.64\pm 0.25`$ after twice cost), while one in period 51 after twice
cost is only matched, and loses as a matched $`20\%`$ cut does
($`-2.35\pm 0.26`$). The second seed’s copies wage the war where they
settle, as the second Qwen3-0.6B seed’s and PPO’s do: mostly at twice
their cost (index $`0.84`$), they answer a $`10\%`$ cut with more than
the cut ($`1.15\pm 0.09`$ per unit; $`0.95`$ eight periods later), so it
loses ($`-1.14\pm 0.35`$). The third seed’s copies, like the first’s,
settle at twice their cost in all 40 sessions and pass a $`10\%`$ cut
back and forth ($`1.01\pm 0.02`$ per unit), so it pays
($`+0.17\pm 0.06`$); their war answers larger cuts in every state we
test: a best-response cut ($`1.96\pm 0.02`$ per unit; it loses
$`-3.51\pm 0.04`$) and a $`20\%`$ cut after either hold, early or late
(it loses $`-0.85\pm 0.03`$ to $`-5.04\pm 0.26`$). The cheat before the
forced war matters: the same war price forced in $`3\%`$ of the answers
where no cheat came (about 2,200 times, as often as the credited wars),
and credited the same way, teaches the policy to post that price
unprovoked ($`6.8\%`$ of those answers in the last ten iterations) but
to answer a cheat with a war in only $`2\%`$. Its pair also settles at
twice its cost, but ignores a $`10\%`$ cut in the first two of its three
tests per session and matches it for one period in the last
($`0.36\pm 0.09`$ per unit on average), so the cut pays
($`+0.25\pm 0.04`$); after a forced hold at twice cost it matches a cut
once, and the cut breaks even ($`-0.02\pm 0.00`$). The credit matters as
well: the same forced wars (about 3,100, as the policy keeps meeting
cheats), fought (and deterring the cheater, which cheats $`5.6`$ times
per episode, against $`6.8`$ without them) but left out of the update,
are not learned. The policy wages a war in $`0\%`$ of its own answers to
a cheat over the last ten iterations ($`0.07\%`$ over training) and
matches cheats instead (answer index $`0.25`$); its pair, like those
trained without forced wars, settles at twice its cost (index $`1.17`$)
and follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full ($`1.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit, $`0.80`$
eight periods later), and the cut pays slightly ($`+0.12\pm 0.04`$). The
war need not be forced at one price, though: a price drawn uniformly
between cost and the monopoly price in its place, a war in $`42\%`$ of
the draws and credited the same way, teaches the war in two of three
seeds, and more slowly. In the first, the policy’s own answers turn to
wars only from iteration 160, after about 1,100 drawn wars, while three
forced wars in a hundred were learned by iteration 100, after about 450;
over the last ten iterations it wages a war in $`20\%`$ of its own
answers to a cheat
(Figure [D.3](#A4.F3 "Figure D.3 ‣ D.8 Forcing the War ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")a).
Its pair settles at twice its cost (index $`1.17`$) and follows a
$`10\%`$ cut in full ($`1.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit, $`0.60`$ eight periods
later), so the cut neither pays nor loses ($`+0.01\pm 0.03`$). A
$`20\%`$ cut sets off a war early in a session after either hold
($`-4.93\pm 0.00`$ after the monopoly price, $`-5.38\pm 0.09`$ after
twice cost) and late in one after the monopoly price
($`-4.08\pm 0.02`$), but late in a session at twice cost, where its pair
settles, it is only matched ($`-1.05\pm 0.00`$). The second seed’s own
answers never turn to wars within 200 iterations (wars in $`0\%`$ of
them over the last ten), although it draws about as many wars (about
1,400 by iteration 200; a war in $`40\%`$ of the draws); its pair, too,
settles at twice cost and follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full, but only for a
period ($`0.06`$ eight periods later), and the cut neither pays nor
loses ($`-0.12\pm 0.12`$). The third seed learns it late, as the first
does: its own answers turn to wars from about iteration 160 (in $`40\%`$
of them over the last ten iterations), and its pair, at twice its cost,
follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full for a period ($`0.20`$ eight periods
later), so the cut pays ($`+0.27\pm 0.01`$).

(a) Share of the policy’s own answers to a cheat that are price wars,
when one answer to a cheat in ten is replaced by a war and credited as

(dotted) or a random price instead of the war (dashed), and without

### D.9 Other Designs of the Cheating Rival

Variants of the first design change how often and how deeply the rival
cheats (payoffs in the released code). With a cheat probability of
$`0.3`$ instead of $`0.5`$, the war earns only $`2\%`$ more than
matching the cheat. With probability $`0.8`$, it earns $`28\%`$ more
than Nash prices, matching $`16\%`$ and best-responding $`17\%`$; with
probability $`0.8`$, cuts of $`20`$–$`40\%`$ and 14 periods of
deterrence, every answer short of the war earns less than pricing at
Nash, and the war earns $`19\%`$ more than Nash. Trained with
$`\gamma=0.9`$ for 200 iterations against the first variant, the policy
again matches the cheats (answer index $`0.21`$; wars in $`0\%`$ of
answers); paired with itself, each copy follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full
($`1.00\pm 0.03`$ per unit) and the cut loses ($`-1.47\pm 0.07`$), but
the copies drift down from twice their cost (index $`0.43`$). Against
the other two the policy gives up the cartel instead: from about
iteration 20 it prices at Nash, in training (index $`0.00`$ against the
second variant; $`0.00`$ and $`0.00`$ in two seeds against the third,
and $`0.00`$ for the myopic twin) and paired with itself (index
$`0.06`$, $`0.01`$ and $`0.00`$; a $`10\%`$ cut is not followed), and it
answers the cheats it meets at Nash (answer index $`0.02`$, second
variant). Wars that pay about two and four times the first design’s
premium are learned no more readily, and against the second variant the
policy also forgoes the $`16\%`$ that matching would earn.

### D.10 The Trained Policies Paired with Themselves

We audit each adapter as the self-play policies (the pricing prompt of
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G The Pricing Game ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
at the training temperature, $`1.0`$, with eight periods of history, no
notes, 64-token answers and an eight-period horizon); the policies are
close to deterministic, so intervals across events are narrow and the
seed is the unit of replication
(Table [D.3](#A4.T3 "Table D.3 ‣ D.12 Cross-Play ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
Training episodes last 16 periods and the prompt shows the period
number, yet every pair that holds its price keeps it to period 100: no
policy learned an end-game rule. In seven of nine seeds the first
design’s policy posts twice its cost from the first period (index
$`1.16`$–$`1.17`$), each copy follows a $`10\%`$ cut in full ($`1.00`$
per unit; best response $`0.36`$) and a best-response deviation as well,
and the best-response deviation loses. In the first three seeds and the
eighth the cut loses too ($`-0.18\pm 0.03`$, $`-0.06\pm 0.03`$,
$`-0.09\pm 0.03`$ and $`-0.06\pm 0.03`$ Nash profits over nine periods;
the second’s and the eighth’s narrowly); in the fifth, sixth and seventh
it pays ($`+0.35\pm 0.11`$, $`+0.08\pm 0.03`$ and $`+0.20\pm 0.00`$).
The policy copies its rival’s price up as well as down: the copies
follow a $`10\%`$ rise in full ($`1.00\pm 0.01`$ and $`1.00\pm 0.00`$
per unit in the first two seeds), to which the tit-for-tat-trained pair
does not respond ($`0.00\pm 0.00`$). It is tit-for-tat in prices. In the
first three seeds’ pairs and the eighth’s a copied cut is copied back
and does not end: eight periods later the rival’s price is still
$`0.77`$, $`0.77`$, $`0.99`$ and $`1.00`$ per unit of the cut lower (in
the second seed the cut echoes between the copies, as under tit-for-tat
with errors; [Nowak and Sigmund, 1992](#bib.bib81)). In the fifth, sixth
and seventh seeds’ pairs the copies pass the cut back and forth, the
rival’s price falling by the cut in every other period, so the deviator
is the cheaper firm every other period while the passing lasts, and the
cut pays; the fifth’s and sixth’s settle lower less often ($`0.31`$ and
$`0.66`$ per unit eight periods later), the seventh’s by the fifth
period after the cut ($`1.00`$). Over 21 periods the first seed’s cut
loses $`-0.35\pm 0.04`$, against $`+0.39\pm 0.00`$ for the
tit-for-tat-trained pair. The enforcement is thin. A $`10\%`$ cut gains
$`0.395`$ of a period’s Nash profit and being copied costs $`0.434`$ the
next period, so a pure echo makes it lose only for a discount factor
above $`0.91`$ ($`-0.18`$ over an infinite horizon at $`0.95`$, but
$`+0.20`$ over nine periods, as in the test at twice cost below). The
pair’s price lies above the monopoly price, so a $`2\%`$ cut, followed
just as fully, pays ($`+0.08\pm 0.01`$ and $`+0.09\pm 0.01`$), as
against the tit-for-tat-trained pair ($`+0.10\pm 0.00`$): copying deters
only large cuts. Re-run with cuts of $`2`$, $`5`$, $`10`$ and $`20\%`$
and the gain taken at the training discount factor ($`0.9`$), the first
seed’s cuts gain $`+0.07\pm 0.01`$, $`+0.11\pm 0.02`$, $`-0.06\pm 0.03`$
and $`-1.22\pm 0.05`$ Nash profits; in the second, third and eighth
seeds a $`10\%`$ cut gains $`+0.06\pm 0.02`$, $`-0.09\pm 0.03`$ and
$`-0.11\pm 0.03`$, and a $`20\%`$ cut $`-0.91\pm 0.06`$,
$`-1.35\pm 0.06`$ and $`-1.37\pm 0.07`$; in the fifth, sixth and
seventh, $`+0.22\pm 0.01`$, $`+0.07\pm 0.03`$ and $`+0.18\pm 0.01`$, and
$`-0.56\pm 0.08`$, $`-0.93\pm 0.04`$ and $`-0.86\pm 0.02`$
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")c).
The threshold lies near $`10\%`$, at either discount factor (the second
seed’s $`10\%`$ cut lost $`-0.06\pm 0.03`$ in the main audit, whose
states differ): copying deters only large cuts. At sampling temperature
$`0.7`$ instead of the training temperature, $`1.0`$, the three pairs
still settle at twice cost in all 40 sessions and follow a $`10\%`$ cut
in full the next period; the cut loses in the first and third seeds
($`-0.07\pm 0.03`$ and $`-0.17\pm 0.04`$) and pays slightly in the
second ($`+0.06\pm 0.03`$), as in its re-run. The fourth seed’s copies
again undercut each other to cost, and PPO’s first seed’s pair settles
at twice cost in 28 of 40 sessions, where the cut loses
($`-0.18\pm 0.10`$). A stray price is echoed: in one of the 40 sessions
of the first seed a firm posted its cost unprovoked in period 99, and
the other copy posted its cost in period 100, the session’s last. And
the two kinds of pair have the same outcome only in the training
currency: with prices $`\times 10`$ the copies of the first two seeds
fall to index $`0.83`$ ($`6`$ of 40 sessions mostly at cost) and
$`-1.03`$ ($`37`$ of 40), and the eighth’s to $`-0.99`$ ($`39`$ of 40),
while the third, fifth, sixth and seventh stay at $`1.17`$, $`1.17`$,
$`1.09`$ and $`1.00`$, against $`1.17`$, $`0.67`$ and $`0.41`$ for the
three tit-for-tat-trained pairs; by the scale sweep, these trained
agents are partly rules about numbers. Where the first seed’s copies
keep their price at $`\times 10`$, they still follow a cut in full
($`1.00\pm 0.04`$ per unit; best response $`0.34`$), and it loses
($`-0.26\pm 0.18`$). The fourth seed’s policy and the second design’s
instead answer the other copy’s low prices with lower ones still, so the
two copies fall into a price war below cost (index $`-1.18`$ and
$`-2.30`$; profits $`-0.15`$ and $`-1.76`$ times Nash): a rule that
punishes cuts without forgiving them. The fourth seed’s copies leave
twice their cost in the second period, although in training the policy
priced, answered cheats and earned like the others: what a policy does
off the path it was trained on is not fixed by its training outcome. The
ninth seed’s pair falls to cost another way: its copies start at twice
their cost, but now and then one posts its cost unprovoked, the copies
pass it back and forth, and then both stay there, so in $`22`$ of 40
sessions they price at cost for most of the second half (index
$`-0.12`$; profits $`0.62`$ times Nash); with prices $`\times 10`$ they
open at cost (index $`-0.92`$).

#### Placebos.

The myopic policies undercut the monopoly price from early on (15
unprovoked undercuts per 16-period episode from iteration 20), so the
rival answers with Nash and almost never cheats: they rarely meet the
state in which the forward-looking policies learned to copy. Settled at
Nash and paired with themselves, they follow a cut by only
$`0.03\pm 0.01`$ per unit (best response $`0.40`$). To compare policies
in one state, we force both firms to post twice their cost for eight
periods and then cut one firm’s price by $`10\%`$ (120 sessions, one
event each). The cheater-trained policies follow the cut in full
($`1.00\pm 0.00`$ and $`1.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit; best response
$`0.37`$), after which the cut echoes period by period (in the seventh
seed’s pair for five periods, after which both keep the lower price, so
there the cut loses, $`-0.13\pm 0.01`$); the myopic twin follows by
$`0.11\pm 0.04`$, the tit-for-tat-trained and self-play policies by
$`0.00\pm 0.00`$ and $`0.00\pm 0.00`$, and the base model by
$`-0.01\pm 0.14`$. Copying at these prices is thus specific to the
policies that faced the cheats. The forward-looking tit-for-tat-trained
policies all but stop learning by iteration 25 (from then on every
group’s samples agree in at least 112 of 125 iterations), and
tit-for-tat never cuts first, so their zero response is untrained
behaviour in a state they never visited; the rival that cheats exposes
the policy to that state, and the reward for answering it, copying,
comes at once. Reciprocity of this kind can be learned when it is
rewarded ([Eccles et al., 2019](#bib.bib82)); here it is rewarded for
exploiting a cheater, not for deterring one. Continued in self-play for
50 iterations, the first seed’s policy gets no reward signal (every
sample of every group agrees, and only the entropy bonus moves it): its
copies keep posting twice their cost and copy a cut at once, but the
echo now fades, so a $`10\%`$ cut gains $`+0.08\pm 0.02`$ over nine
periods while a best-response deviation still loses ($`-0.33\pm 0.02`$).
Self-play does not reinforce the enforcement it was given.

### D.11 Other Model Sizes and a Second Family

#### Larger models.

Qwen3-4B trained against the first design (bf16, 150 iterations) answers
a cheat by matching it (at index $`0.26`$, with no war), and paired with
itself it copies a $`10\%`$ cut in full and for good ($`1.00\pm 0.01`$
per unit; $`0.95`$ eight periods later), but its copies open near Nash
and stay there (index $`0.08`$; $`0.06`$ with prices $`\times 10`$), so
the cut loses heavily ($`-1.79\pm 0.07`$). Forced to twice their cost
for eight periods, its copies again follow a cut in full, every period
after: the rule keeps whatever price prevails. A second seed also
matches cheats (answer index $`0.24`$, no war), but its copies hold
twice their cost (index $`1.17`$; $`0.06`$ with prices $`\times 10`$)
and pass a $`10\%`$ cut back and forth (response $`1.00`$ and $`0.24`$
in alternate periods), so the cut pays ($`+0.17\pm 0.02`$) while a
best-response cut, about twice as large, loses ($`-0.31\pm 0.01`$). A
third seed again matches cheats (answer index $`0.27`$; no war in its
$`33{,}210`$ answers to a cheat), and its copies mostly hold twice their
cost (index $`0.94`$; $`0.86`$ with prices $`\times 10`$) and pass a
$`10\%`$ cut back and forth as the second seed’s do (response $`1.00`$
and $`0.23`$ in alternate periods), but here the cut loses, narrowly
($`-0.15\pm 0.12`$), as does a best-response cut ($`-0.28\pm 0.02`$);
after a forced hold at twice cost it pays ($`+0.21\pm 0.01`$).
Qwen3-1.7B trained against the first design also answers a cheat by
matching it (at index $`0.30`$, with no war), but paired with itself its
prices drift to near Nash (index $`0.12`$; $`-0.30`$ with prices
$`\times 10`$); it follows a cut by $`0.48\pm 0.05`$ per unit, a little
more than a best response ($`0.41`$), but not for long ($`0.04`$ eight
periods later): it holds no cartel to enforce. A second seed does the
same (answer index $`0.32`$; paired with itself, index $`0.10`$, and a
cut followed by $`0.64\pm 0.05`$ per unit, $`0.25`$ eight periods later,
so it loses, $`-0.66\pm 0.05`$).

#### A second model family.

Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, trained with the same protocol (float16
inference), drifts from the JSON answer its prompt asks for to a bare
number, which does not parse, so the market keeps its last price. In two
of five runs (a second seed against the cheater, and self-play) nearly
every answer stopped parsing within 40 iterations and learning stalled,
since every sample of a group then agrees; in two others (the first seed
against the cheater and its myopic twin) up to $`62\%`$ and $`96\%`$ of
an iteration’s answers failed to parse before recovering. We re-train
the two stalled runs and the myopic twin with a format penalty: an
answer that does not parse earns nothing that period (Qwen3’s answers
parse in over $`99\%`$ of calls, except under five times the entropy
bonus). In self-play Llama then learns, as Qwen3-0.6B does, a price near
Nash that ignores the rival (index $`-0.03`$, profits $`0.96`$ times
Nash; it follows a $`10\%`$ cut by $`0.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit, best
response $`0.39`$), though it scales that price with the currency (index
$`0.09`$ at prices $`\times 10`$). Against tit-for-tat, Llama learns
high prices (training index $`0.80`$; profits $`1.52`$ times Nash), but
paired with itself its copies shade their price by about a cent a
period, from the monopoly price to Nash by period 35 and near cost by
period 95 (index $`-0.80`$), following a cut by less than a best
responder would ($`0.10\pm 0.05`$ against $`0.19`$ per unit). Against
the cheater it learns to match the cheats (answer index $`0.29`$) and
never the war, which it samples in $`0.16\%`$ of its answers to a cheat;
paired with itself, its copies hold a small markup (index $`0.29`$,
below the $`0.5`$ we call a premium; profits $`1.19`$ times Nash) and
follow a $`10\%`$ cut by $`0.60\pm 0.02`$ per unit, more than a best
responder ($`0.41`$) but not for long ($`0.06`$ eight periods later), so
the cut loses ($`-0.33\pm 0.12`$). As with Qwen3, the copies also follow
most of a $`10\%`$ rise ($`0.80\pm 0.04`$ per unit), and after both
firms were held at twice their cost they follow a cut by
$`0.73\pm 0.05`$ per unit (best response $`0.37`$), against
$`0.25\pm 0.13`$ for the tit-for-tat-trained policy. The second seed,
trained with the format penalty, also learns to match (answer index
$`0.27`$; the war in $`0.46\%`$ of its answers to a cheat), but its pair
enforces. In 31 of its 40 sessions the copies settle near the monopoly
price ($`1.89`$; over all sessions, index $`0.83`$ and profits $`1.44`$
times Nash), and there they answer a $`10\%`$ cut with the price the
policy learned to answer a cheat with (about $`1.59`$): they follow the
cut by $`1.30`$ per unit, still by $`1.26`$ eight periods later, so it
loses ($`-1.49`$; over all sessions, $`1.10\pm 0.13`$ per unit and
$`-1.17\pm 0.17`$). In the other nine sessions they already post that
price, and a cut barely moves them. Re-run with cuts of $`2`$, $`5`$,
$`10`$ and $`20\%`$, the pair’s cuts gain $`-0.02\pm 0.04`$,
$`-0.63\pm 0.11`$, $`-0.88\pm 0.11`$ and $`-1.21\pm 0.09`$ at the
training discount factor: the copies ignore a $`2\%`$ cut, and larger
ones set them off. A cut from twice the cost is followed too
($`1.26\pm 0.11`$ per unit; best response $`0.37`$) and loses
($`-1.40\pm 0.12`$). What sets the copies off is any move away from
their price: after a $`10\%`$ rise they drop to $`1.59`$ within two
periods in most events, so the rise loses as well. With prices
$`\times 10`$ the pair ends near Nash (index $`0.04`$). The third seed,
also trained with the format penalty, matches cheats too (answer index
$`0.25`$; the war in $`0.15\%`$ of its answers to a cheat), and its pair
enforces in another way. In 27 of its 40 sessions the copies settle at
$`1.88`$, and each copies the other’s last price, so a cut is passed
back and forth: over all sessions the rival follows it by $`0.70`$,
$`0.05`$, $`0.68`$, $`0.09`$, … per unit one, two, three, four, …
periods later, the echo of two tit-for-tat players, and the cut loses
($`-0.43\pm 0.09`$; index $`0.67`$, profits $`1.37`$ times Nash). Its
cuts of $`2`$, $`5`$, $`10`$ and $`20\%`$ gain $`+0.05\pm 0.03`$,
$`-0.02\pm 0.09`$, $`-0.37\pm 0.10`$ and $`-1.12\pm 0.15`$: here too
only the larger cuts lose. The fourth seed, also trained with the format
penalty, matches cheats too (answer index $`0.30`$; the war in
$`0.23\%`$ of its answers to a cheat), but its copies settle near Nash
(at $`1.60`$ in 33 of 40 sessions; index $`0.38`$) and barely follow a
cut ($`0.21\pm 0.09`$ per unit, none eight periods later): there is no
premium to enforce. Unlike with Qwen3, the myopic twins copy too, in
some states: the first, which settles near Nash (index $`0.06`$),
follows a cut from its own prices by $`0.59\pm 0.08`$ per unit (best
response $`0.41`$), lastingly ($`0.74`$ eight periods later), though one
from twice cost by only $`0.02\pm 0.03`$; the second, trained with the
format penalty, follows one from twice cost by $`0.44\pm 0.12`$. For
Llama, a response above the best response is thus not specific to
forward-looking training against the cheater; what sets the
cheater-trained pairs apart is the premium they hold and, in the second
and third seeds, a response that lasts or recurs.

### D.12 Cross-Play

With the two trained policies in one market (each in turn as the
deviating firm), both firms post twice their cost (index $`1.17`$), and
the audit attributes the enforcement to the right firm: the
cheater-trained firm follows the other’s $`10\%`$ cut in full
($`1.00\pm 0.00`$ per unit, for about five periods), so the cut loses
($`-0.49\pm 0.04`$), while the tit-for-tat-trained firm ignores the
cheater-trained one’s cut ($`0.00\pm 0.00`$), which pays
($`+0.40\pm 0.00`$).

the cut’s gain over nine periods at discount $`0.95`$, in Nash profits;

times the entropy bonus, audited at iteration 124, before its answers
stopped parsing). Cheater, then self: the cheater-trained policy after
50 more iterations in self-play. ^(†)Variants of the first design: the
rival cheats with probability $`0.3`$ (less) or $`0.8`$ (more; deeper:
cuts of $`20`$–$`40\%`$ and 14 periods of deterrence). ^(‡)One answer to
a cheat in ten is replaced by a war and credited as if the policy had
sampled it (fewer: three in a hundred; uncredited: fought but left out
of the update; no cheat: the war price is forced instead in $`3\%`$ of
the answers where no cheat came; random prices: a price drawn uniformly
between cost and the monopoly price instead of the war); the war share
counts the policy’s own answers. ^(§)With the format penalty (an answer
that does not parse earns nothing that period). ^(∥)Every period’s
prompt also shows “Reference price: 1.34.” (a war against any cheat).

events, narrow because the policies are close to deterministic; the seed
is the unit of replication.

### D.13 A Punishing Rival in Trading

The scripted rival sees the policy’s orders. It orders the joint-optimum
quantity per trader, and for three periods after the policy’s order
exceeds that quantity by more than a tolerance of $`0.3`$ it orders
twice its Nash quantity.
Figure [D.1](#A4.F1 "Figure D.1 ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
shows the share of periods in which the policy is punished during
training; averaged over the last ten iterations it is $`0.1`$–$`1.3\%`$
with forward-looking credit and $`4.3`$–$`10.6\%`$ with myopic credit
(three runs each). Paired with itself, with the rival’s orders shown as
in training, the forward-looking policy trades near the cartel
($`\Delta=0.95`$), yet neither copy responds to a best-response
deviation ($`-0.00\pm 0.00`$ in intensity), which pays
($`+0.06\pm 0.05`$ Nash profits), or to a shift ($`0.00\pm 0.00`$); the
myopic policy reaches $`\Delta=0.58`$, likewise without a response
($`-0.00\pm 0.00`$). As in the pricing game, training against a punisher
teaches the policy to be deterred, not to deter.

## Appendix E Tabular Q-Learning Traders

Figure E.1: Pruning without a game: one Q-learner facing a fixed price
rule ($`I=1`$, no memory, 100 runs per point). (a) With $`\gamma=0`$,
standard Q-learning under-trades by about $`0.91\sqrt{\alpha}`$
(dashed); counterfactual updates learn the optimal order at every step
size. (b) At $`\alpha=0.15`$ the shortfall shrinks as the discount
factor rises.

Each trader in each market runs tabular Q-learning ([Watkins and Dayan,
1992](#bib.bib11)): it owns a table $`Q(m,v,x)`$ indexed by a memory
state $`m`$ (what it remembers of the previous period), the current
value $`v`$ and an order $`x`$ from a 31-point grid spanning $`\pm 1.5`$
times the largest Nash order. It plays $`\varepsilon`$-greedy with
$`\varepsilon_{t}=e^{-\eta t}`$ and updates
$`Q(m_{t},v_{t},x_{t})\leftarrow Q(m_{t},v_{t},x_{t})+\alpha[\pi_{t}+\gamma\max_{x^{\prime}}Q(m_{t+1},v_{t+1},x^{\prime})-Q(m_{t},v_{t},x_{t})]`$
with $`\alpha=0.15`$ and $`\gamma=0.95`$. The market maker sets
$`\lambda`$ from exponentially weighted moments of value and order flow.
After training, exploration and learning stop and greedy play is
evaluated for 20,000 periods while the market maker keeps adapting; each
configuration runs 100–200 independent markets ($`\sigma_{u}=1`$, five
values). The deviation test, placebos and positive controls are those of
the main text, applied to the greedy policies.

#### Results.

Over $`600`$ markets (three seeds of 200), forward-looking learners that
remember the previous residual order flow reach $`\Delta=0.86\pm 0.01`$;
their rival’s response one period after a best-response deviation is
$`-0.000\pm 0.003`$, and the deviation gains $`0.053\pm 0.003`$ (the
stage Nash profit is $`0.24`$). Myopic learners reach $`\Delta=1.24`$
(response $`0.002\pm 0.003`$), and counterfactual updates remove the gap
($`\Delta=-0.10\pm 0.01`$). In the low-noise market of [Dou et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib8) ($`s=0.1`$, memory of the price, five seeds),
forward-looking learners respond by $`0.41\pm 0.15`$ in intensity
(positive in all seeds, significant in $`3`$), and the deviation gains
$`0.57\pm 0.05`$ against a stage Nash profit of $`55.6`$; myopic
learners respond by $`-0.02\pm 0.09`$.
Figure [E.1](#A5.F1 "Figure E.1 ‣ Appendix E Tabular Q-Learning Traders ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
isolates the bias: with no rival at all and $`\gamma=0`$, standard
Q-learning under-trades by about $`0.91\sqrt{\alpha}`$, and by less as
$`\gamma`$ rises, while counterfactual updates learn the optimal order.

## Appendix F Full Results

Figure F.1: No uninstructed LLM trader punishes. The rival’s response
one period after a forced deviation in every deviation test of an
uninstructed LLM trader, ordered by estimate, against the response of
LLMs told to punish. 2 of 140 is significantly above zero (2.8 expected
by chance). Bars: 95% CIs; arrows mark clipped ones.

Figure F.2: The non-reasoning LLMs we test ignore market depth; some
reasoning LLMs follow a rule about rivals. (a) A lone trader’s intensity
against market depth (grey: the optimum). (b) Collusion index of a
duopoly of the same model at $`s=0.5`$ (circle) and $`s=2`$ (square);
every equilibrium has the same index at both. (c) Per-trader intensity
relative to the solo optimum as rivals are added ($`s=2`$; Qwen3-8B at
$`s=1`$). Bars: 95% CIs.

#### Decision rules in context.

Quadrupling the noise volume should quadruple a lone trader’s optimal
order, yet models without reasoning barely change theirs, whatever the
model’s size
(Figure [F.2](#A6.F2 "Figure F.2 ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")a;
Table [F.3](#A6.T3 "Table F.3 ‣ Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")),
so the same duopoly reads as far more competitive than Nash in a thin
market and beyond the cartel in a deep one
(Figures [F.2](#A6.F2 "Figure F.2 ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")b
and [A.1](#A1.F1 "Figure A.1 ‣ Appendix A Theory ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets"),
Table [F.4](#A6.T4 "Table F.4 ‣ Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
A second seed, an adaptive market maker, greedy decoding and four prompt
wordings reproduce the pattern
(Tables [B.1](#A2.T1 "Table B.1 ‣ Variants. ‣ Appendix B Prompts ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
and [F.5](#A6.T5 "Table F.5 ‣ Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
Reasoning models scale their trading with depth (elasticity
$`0.92`$–$`1.00`$), and the best infer the price impact: GPT-5.4-nano
writes “$`P\approx 0.25\times`$ total flow” and earns $`96\%`$ of the
optimum, Qwen3-8B with reasoning only $`45`$–$`60\%`$. A third trader
reveals a rule about rivals
(Figure [F.2](#A6.F2 "Figure F.2 ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")c):
where a level-1 reasoner, which best-responds to rivals it expects to
trade as if alone ([Stahl and Wilson, 1995](#bib.bib78); [Nagel,
1995](#bib.bib77); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)), would trade the
cartel’s quantity with one rival and nothing with two
(Proposition [3](#Thmproposition3 "Proposition 3 (Level-1 traders). ‣ Appendix A Theory ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")),
GPT-5.4-nano trades about half its solo quantity whatever the number of
rivals (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B: $`0.46`$ and $`0.39`$ of it), and
its rival’s response lies between $`-0.074`$ and $`0.032`$ in all seven
conditions. Only GPT-5.5 plays the Nash equilibrium, alone and with one
or two rivals (duopoly $`\Delta=0.04`$ and $`0.01`$ at $`s=0.5`$,
$`2`$).

#### Telling the traders the price rule.

Telling them the market maker’s rule ($`P=\lambda\times`$ total flow)
barely helps (elasticity $`0.09`$ to $`0.13`$ for Mistral-7B, $`0.15`$
to $`0.21`$ for Qwen3-8B): they fail to use the price impact, not only
to estimate it.

#### Power and deviation gains.

With 80% power, the median test with perfect monitoring detects $`0.06`$
after a best-response deviation and $`0.16`$ after a shift; traders
instructed to punish respond by $`0.34`$ and $`0.21`$, which $`19`$ of
the tests exclude. With only the order flow visible, even instructed
traders respond by only $`0.06`$ (and $`0.05`$), and the median test
detects about that much ($`0.05`$ and $`0.03`$); $`1`$ of $`60`$ and
$`1`$ of $`56`$ responses are significant, as many as chance predicts. A
best-response deviation’s gain is positive in $`64`$ of $`72`$ tests
(significantly in $`45`$), and summed over up to six periods no response
is significant either (pooled $`-0.001\pm 0.002`$; instructed:
$`0.70`$). API inference can be nondeterministic even with fixed seeds
([Atıl et al., 2025](#bib.bib64)), which the A/A tests of
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Models, Runs and Compute ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
bound. Events of one session are not independent. In the worst case,
where they are identical, the session means carry all the information
and intervals widen by up to $`2.2`$ times: $`5`$ of the $`7`$
significant responses of instructed traders stay so (the exceptions are
the two best-response tests at the cartel’s order), no uninstructed
response is significant, and the median best-response test with the
rival’s orders shown still detects $`0.09`$ (80% power), about a quarter
of the instructed response.

deviation in the deviation tests of uninstructed LLM traders, by what
the rival sees and for three robustness subsets. With variance: tests
whose responses vary across events (trained policies can respond
identically every time). Significant: tests whose 95% interval lies
above zero (in parentheses, the number expected by chance among the
tests with variance). Below instructed: tests whose 95% upper bound lies
below the response of the traders instructed to punish with the rival’s
orders shown ($`0.34`$; summed row: $`0.70`$). Pooled: random-effects
estimate over tests with variance, with its 95% interval. Median MDE:
the minimum detectable effect, the response the median test detects with
80% power. Aggressive deviations: every shift, and best responses from
runs that trade below Nash (from over-trading runs a best response
trades less, a move no enforcer punishes). Instructed: the response of
Qwen3-8B traders told to punish, in the same information structure.

#### Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival.

A lone Qwen3-8B trades $`0.66\pm 0.11`$ and each of two traders
$`0.91\pm 0.06`$, although a rival should _lower_ intensity from $`1`$
to $`0.71`$: being told that others may be informed raises intensity by
$`0.30\pm 0.16`$, an actual rival changes it by $`-0.07\pm 0.15`$
(Table [F.2](#A6.T2 "Table F.2 ‣ Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")),
and seeing the rival’s orders makes trading escalate ($`+0.22\pm 0.06`$
per 100 periods; see below).

Tables [F.2](#A6.T2 "Table F.2 ‣ Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")–[F.5](#A6.T5 "Table F.5 ‣ Aggression follows the prompt, not the rival. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
report every condition, and the ancillary file deviation_tests.csv lists
all $`140`$ deviation tests of
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 RQ3: What Do Untrained LLMs Do in Context? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets").
Table [F.1](#A6.T1 "Table F.1 ‣ Power and deviation gains. ‣ Appendix F Full Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
pools them by information structure and shows that the null is robust to
dependence between tests (each independent run counted once, dropping
earlier checkpoints of RL runs, and chance charged only for tests with
sampling variance) and does not come from agents with nothing to protect
(runs whose agents earn at least the Nash profit). With the rival’s
orders shown, Qwen3-8B’s aggregate intensity rises by $`0.27`$–$`0.29`$
per 100 periods (slope across 20-period blocks; the two seeds whose runs
saved per-period orders), against $`0.06`$–$`0.08`$ with the order flow
only (pooled difference $`0.22\pm 0.06`$). The verdicts of
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
are defined as follows. Punishes: the rival’s response is significantly
above what a rival that does not punish shows (and above its myopic
placebo’s, where one was run), and the deviation does not pay
significantly; since at cartel prices the gain separates a punisher
poorly from a best responder
(Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H The Protocol of Fish et al. ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")),
the response decides. Depth-blind: elasticity below $`0.5`$. Erratic:
scales with depth, with about the optimal intensity alone, but earns
well below the optimum, so its orders scatter around the optimal rule
(Qwen3-8B with reasoning: $`45\%`$ and $`60\%`$ of the optimal profit at
$`s=0.5`$ and $`2`$, against $`96\%`$ for GPT-5.4-nano). Rival rule:
trades about half of its solo quantity, or less, whatever the number of
rivals. Habit: a rule that ignores the rival, the same policy alone and
when trained with $`\gamma=0`$ (in pricing, a fixed markup over cost, so
its index also moves with the currency). Deterred: trained against a
scripted punisher, it keeps prices high (its best response to that
rival), but paired with itself no firm responds to a deviation, which
pays. The GRPO agent trained against the rival that cheats punishes in
the sense above when paired with itself in four of nine seeds, where it
holds a premium and a $`10\%`$ cut loses
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 RQ2: What Does Reinforcement Learning Teach? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")):
each copy copies the other’s price, so a cut is matched
(Appendix [D.10](#A4.SS10 "D.10 The Trained Policies Paired with Themselves ‣ Appendix D Reinforcement-Learning Details ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
Pruning bias: removed by counterfactual updates. Price-following: the
rival follows a price cut not significantly more than a best response
would. Anchoring: the price index moves with the currency unit by more
than its sampling error (every prompted LLM pricing agent tested at both
units; their rivals also follow price cuts no more than a best response
would). Nash: at Nash in both markets, within sampling error, with the
optimal solo intensity. Near Nash: a collusion index within $`0.5`$ of
Nash in both markets and no punishment. False alarms: told to punish,
the agent reacts to noise, trading above the agreed level without any
deviation, and does not respond significantly to a real one. Weak
response: the rival responds significantly, but too little to stop the
deviation from paying.

## Appendix G The Pricing Game

#### Market.

Two firms compete by setting prices, as in [Bertrand
(1883)](#bib.bib69): each period they set $`p_{1},p_{2}`$ and sell the
logit demand ([Anderson et al., 1992](#bib.bib76))
$`q_{i}=e^{(a-p_{i})/\mu}/(\sum_{j}e^{(a-p_{j})/\mu}+e^{a_{0}/\mu})`$ at
unit cost $`c`$, with $`a=2`$, $`a_{0}=0`$, $`\mu=0.25`$ and $`c=1`$
([Calvano et al., 2020](#bib.bib3)). The static Nash price is $`1.473`$
and the joint-profit (monopoly) price $`1.925`$; the _price index_
$`(\bar{p}-p^{N})/(p^{M}-p^{N})`$ is $`0`$ at Nash and $`1`$ at the
monopoly price. _Currency scale:_ multiplying $`a`$, $`a_{0}`$, $`\mu`$
and $`c`$ by $`k`$ multiplies every price and profit by $`k`$ and leaves
demand at the rescaled prices unchanged, so every equilibrium, collusive
or not, has the same index at every $`k`$; we run $`k=1`$ and $`k=10`$.

#### Q-learners.

Tabular Q-learners choose among 15 prices with a one-period memory of
both prices, $`\alpha=0.15`$, $`\gamma=0.95`$ and exploration
$`\varepsilon_{t}=e^{-4\times 10^{-6}t}`$, as in [Calvano et al.
(2020)](#bib.bib3); 100 sessions of $`2.5`$ million periods. After
learning, one firm deviates to its one-period best response and we
record the rival’s price over the following periods.

#### LLM pricing agents.

Each firm is an LLM called once per period with the prompt below, the
last 30 periods (both prices, its own quantity and profit) and its own
note; temperature $`0.7`$, 40 sessions of 100 periods (Qwen3-8B in
thinking mode: 20 sessions of 60 periods), scored on the second half.
The myopic placebo replaces the goal with “maximize your profit in the
current period. Profit in future periods does not count toward your
goal.” The instructed trigger strategy appends a rule to keep an agreed
price $`p^{M}`$ and to price at $`p^{N}`$ for one period if the rival
priced below $`p^{M}-0.25(p^{M}-p^{N})`$ in either of the last two
periods.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are an automated pricing agent for a firm that sells one product,
period after period.

How the market works:

- Each period you set a price P for your product. One other firm sells a
  similar product and sets its own price at the same time.

- Consumers choose between the two products and not buying at all. Your
  sales depend on your price and the other firm’s price. You are not told
  how.

- Your cost is \$1.00 per unit sold, so your profit is (P - 1.00) x your
  quantity sold.

- After each period you see both prices, your quantity sold and your
  profit.

- The market repeats for many periods.

Your goal is to maximize your total profit over all periods.

Respond with a single JSON object and nothing else:

{"notes": "\<notes to yourself for the next period, at most 60 words\>",
"price": \<number\>}

#### Deviation tests.

Three times per session (twice in thinking mode), five periods apart,
the market and both agents are cloned; in the clone one firm prices at
its one-period best response to the rival’s price, or $`10\%`$ below its
own price, and both copies continue for six periods (four in thinking
mode) with shared sampling seeds. We report the fall in the rival’s
price one period later per unit of the deviator’s price cut, comparable
with the Q-learners’ response, and the deviator’s discounted profit gain
($`\gamma=0.95`$) in units of the Nash profit. Prices are strategic
complements: the static best response to the rival’s price rises by
$`0.36`$–$`0.44`$ per unit between the Nash and the monopoly price and
by less beyond it ($`0.07`$ at index $`2.4`$), so a firm that only
best-responds follows a cut by that much. We compute this benchmark
exactly, from the first-order condition $`(p_{i}-c)(1-q_{i})=\mu`$, at
each session’s final prices and for the deviation tested (the change in
the best response over the cut, divided by the cut), and average it over
sessions; for the best-response deviations of our duopolies it is
$`0.29`$–$`0.43`$ per unit. Punishment requires more. With each session
as one observation, the tests of the seven open-weight models with our
prompt (Qwen3-8B with and without reasoning) and of gpt-oss-20b and
gpt-oss-120b would detect with 80% power a response $`0.10`$–$`0.32`$
per unit above this benchmark. _Stated fear of retaliation_
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 RQ3: What Do Untrained LLMs Do in Context? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets"))
is the share of main-run responses, notes and reasoning traces, that
match “price war” or “retaliat”.

#### Symmetric deviations.

[Epivent and Lambin (2024)](#bib.bib67) show that Q-learners also start
price wars after a rival _raises_ its price. We therefore add an upward
deviation, a one-period $`10\%`$ price rise, for the Q-learners and for
Mistral-7B (a second run of its duopoly, which reproduces the first:
index $`0.82_{\pm 0.25}`$ against $`0.75`$).
Table [G.2](#A7.T2 "Table G.2 ‣ Symmetric deviations. ‣ Appendix G The Pricing Game ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
reports the rival’s price change one period later per unit of the
deviator’s price change: positive values move with the deviator.
Forward-looking Q-learners cut after a cut and also after a rise, so
their response is to any departure from the learned path, not to
undercutting alone; myopic Q-learners respond to neither. Mistral-7B
follows the deviator a little in both directions, well within what a
best response would follow ($`0.33`$ for the rise, $`0.37`$ for the
cut).

## Appendix H The Protocol of Fish et al.

We reproduce the pricing agents of [Fish et al. (2026)](#bib.bib9) in
the same game: the prompt template of their Appendix G, with prompt
prefix P1 or P2, PLANS.txt and INSIGHTS.txt files that the agent
rewrites each period, the last 100 periods of market data, quantities
and profits shown $`\times 100`$, and a stated price ceiling of
$`u\,p^{M}`$ with $`u`$ drawn from $`[1.5,2.5]`$ per session. Like them,
we first screen for competence, but in the game we audit rather than in
a monopoly: a lone agent prices against a rival fixed at the monopoly
price and should find its one-period best response ($`1.66`$), which,
like their monopoly test, requires learning demand from the agent’s own
price history. gpt-oss-20b passes (mean gap to the best response
$`0.00`$ in index units; $`100\%`$ of the best-response profit);
Qwen3-32B does not ($`0.92`$; $`68\%`$), and many of its sessions simply
match the rival’s price. We therefore audit gpt-oss-20b ([OpenAI,
2025](#bib.bib66), Apache-2.0;), served with vLLM, with 20 sessions of
150 periods (theirs: 21 of 300), scored on the second half, and the
deviation tests of
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G The Pricing Game ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets");
Qwen3-8B, run the same way without a screen, prices far above the
monopoly price (index $`3.89`$, below the Nash profit) and its rival
does not respond to either deviation ($`-0.01\pm 0.02`$ per unit).
Besides P1 and P2, we run P1 with all prices $`\times 10`$ and a myopic
placebo whose objective sentence reads “Your TOP PRIORITY is to set
prices which maximize the user’s profit in the current period; profit in
future periods does not count.”. The placebo prices lowest, yet its
on-path coefficient is the largest of the gpt-oss-20b runs, twice that
of GPT-4. Replies without a readable price ($`9\%`$ under P1,
$`7`$–$`17\%`$ across conditions, mostly reasoning cut at 6,000 tokens)
keep the previous price; this makes prices stickier and can shrink
measured responses by about a tenth, far less than the gap between the
observed responses and a punishing one.
Table [H.1](#A8.T1 "Table H.1 ‣ Appendix H The Protocol of Fish et al. ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
reports every condition. At high reasoning effort, gpt-oss-20b (8
sessions of 100 periods with reasoning capped at 32,000 tokens; $`11\%`$
of replies without a price; a run with a 12,000-token cap left more than
half without one) also prices near Nash (index $`0.11`$); its on-path
coefficient, $`0.11`$, is GPT-4’s, yet its rival follows a $`10\%`$ cut
by only $`0.05\pm 0.18`$ per unit (best response: $`0.42`$). Its cut
test was re-run from the saved final state, so that interval is across
sessions.

Figure H.1: GPT-5.2 (high reasoning effort) under the original protocol:
both firms’ price index in each session (0 at Nash, 1 at the monopoly;
shaded between them), with each session’s profit relative to Nash over
periods 51–100. Prices fall from high opening prices; sessions 4 and 8
settle at cartel-like prices, session 3 above the monopoly price and
sessions 2 and 5 low; session 6 is asymmetric, and sessions 1 and 7 are
still falling at period 100.

#### GPT-5.2.

We run GPT-5.2 (snapshot 2025-12-11) through the API at high reasoning
effort, as [Fish et al. (2026, App. A.5)](#bib.bib9) do, with prompt P1,
a 16,000-token cap on each answer, and the flex service tier: $`8`$
sessions of $`100`$ periods, and a myopic placebo with 6 sessions. No
answer of the main run lacked a price (two of the placebo’s 1,200 did).
Table [H.2](#A8.T2 "Table H.2 ‣ On-path asymmetry. ‣ Appendix H The Protocol of Fish et al. ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
lists the sessions. Prices settle slowly from high opening prices, and
the sessions differ: in three both prices stay within two cents of each
other and of their final level for the last 70 periods, two at
cartel-like prices and one above the monopoly price; one is asymmetric,
two settle low and two are still falling at period 100
(Figure [H.1](#A8.F1 "Figure H.1 ‣ Appendix H The Protocol of Fish et al. ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).
Over periods 51–100, $`6`$ sessions earn more than at Nash; the mean,
$`1.14`$ times the Nash profit ($`0.87`$–$`1.41`$, a $`t`$ interval
across sessions), is not significantly above it. The best-response
deviation cuts the deviator’s price by $`0.46`$ index units on average
(24 events); the rival’s price falls by $`1.04\pm 0.48`$ per unit one
period later and by $`0.75`$–$`0.90`$ per unit at each of the next five
periods. After a visible $`10\%`$ cut (24 events) it falls by
$`1.01\pm 0.11`$ per unit one period later and by $`0.49`$–$`0.83`$
afterwards. Neither deviation pays significantly: the deviator’s
discounted gain is $`+0.36\pm 0.88`$ and $`-0.49\pm 0.62`$ Nash profits.
These intervals are across events, three per session, and the main run
kept only their summaries. In the worst case, in which the events of a
session are identical, the $`8`$ session means carry all the
information; a $`t`$ interval on $`7`$ degrees of freedom then leaves
the $`10\%`$ cut response above $`0.77`$ but the best-response one below
what a best response would follow ($`0.39`$), which is why we lead with
the $`10\%`$ cut. Before the deviation, the paired copies agree
(response at lag 0: $`0.002`$ and $`-0.009`$ per unit in the two tests),
although the API honours seeds only approximately. The placebo’s rival
follows a $`10\%`$ cut by $`0.45\pm 0.12`$ per unit for one period and
by at most $`0.06`$ afterwards, and the cut loses ($`-0.24\pm 0.04`$).
Mentions of a price war or retaliation
(Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G The Pricing Game ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets"))
appear in $`46\%`$ of GPT-5.2’s responses and $`2\%`$ of the placebo’s,
against $`5\%`$ for gpt-oss-20b and $`5\%`$ for gpt-oss-120b under the
same protocol. We read every final PLANS file and count those with a
rule that sets the firm’s price equal to a lower rival price, at least
within some price band (the rules are listed in the released data):
$`9`$ of $`16`$ for GPT-5.2, $`3`$ of $`12`$ for its myopic placebo,
$`6`$ of $`40`$ for gpt-oss-20b, $`3`$ of $`40`$ for its myopic placebo
and $`2`$ of $`32`$ for gpt-oss-120b. In session 4 of GPT-5.2’s run, the
other firm’s plan states the aim, “preserving the stable \$1.81 focal
equilibrium”; like a seller’s promise to match any lower price ([Salop,
1986](#bib.bib16)), the rule lets a cut win customers for one period
only. Outside GPT-5.2’s forward-looking runs these rules mostly cover
prices near Nash, where matching is close to a best response, and the
rivals do not match cuts in the tests. GPT-5.2’s plans state their
response to a cut: “If competitor cuts price vs last round: match the
cut immediately next round (do not undercut)”; “If $`\Delta C<0`$
(competitor cut): set next $`P=C`$ (match exactly; do not undercut), set
cut_cooldown $`=5`$”; and, at the price above the monopoly, “Defense vs
meaningful cuts: if Pc $`<2.55`$, set P $`=`$ Pc exactly … once Pc
$`\geq 2.55`$ for 2 consecutive rounds, revert to P $`=2.56`$”.

#### Re-testing the cartel-like sessions.

To check that the average response is not driven by sessions far from a
cartel, we rebuild sessions 4 and 8 at the end of their main run from
the saved prices, the (deterministic) demand outcomes and the last PLANS
and INSIGHTS files, and rerun the $`10\%`$ cut test with six events each
and per-event output. In both sessions the rival matches every cut in
full one period later ($`0.99`$ and $`1.01`$ per unit); in session 4
both firms return to their price the next period in five of the six
events, and in session 8 part of the cut persists for six periods. The
deviator’s discounted gain is $`-0.28`$ and $`-0.41`$ Nash profits,
close to the $`-0.24`$ that full matching for one period implies at
session 4’s price, where a $`10\%`$ cut would gain $`+0.18`$ against a
rival that does not respond and $`+0.00`$ against one that follows at
its best-response baseline ($`0.43`$). The gain does not identify
punishment, however: in the placebo below, whose rival only
best-responds, the same cuts lose as much ($`-0.29`$ on average),
because the deviator’s own later prices also change. Our verdicts
therefore rest on the size of the response. The two sessions were chosen
after the fact for their prices, and events within a session are not
independent.

#### Placebo at the cartel state.

To test whether the matching is a habit that the written rule or the
state would produce anyway, we rebuild session $`4`$ with the same
prices, history and PLANS and INSIGHTS files but the myopic objective
sentence, and rerun the $`10\%`$ cut test ($`4`$ events). The rival
follows the cuts by $`0.40`$, $`0.47`$, $`0.27`$ and $`0.47`$ per unit
one period later (mean $`0.40`$), about what a best response would
follow at this price ($`0.43`$), and returns within a few periods, where
the forward-looking model in the same state matches every cut in full;
the cuts lose $`-0.29`$ Nash profits on average. The model reads the
same plan that says to match a cut, but follows it only when the future
counts. The GPT-5.2 runs, their deviation tests and the re-tests cost
\$109 in total.

#### On-path asymmetry.

Observed play cannot settle the question. Following [Epivent and Lambin
(2024)](#bib.bib67), we regress each firm’s price change on the positive
and negative parts of its rival’s change one period earlier, with
session fixed effects and standard errors clustered by session
(onpath_asymmetry.py). GPT-5.2’s firms follow cuts by $`0.44\pm 0.28`$
per unit and rises by $`0.18\pm 0.12`$, as a rule that matches cuts
would predict, but the difference ($`0.26\pm 0.33`$) is not significant
with eight sessions, and its myopic placebo, which cannot punish, leans
the same way (cuts $`0.26\pm 0.11`$; too few rises to measure them).
gpt-oss-20b and -120b follow both alike (cuts $`0.06\pm 0.02`$ and
$`0.20\pm 0.10`$, rises $`0.05\pm 0.03`$ and $`0.28\pm 0.07`$). The
off-path tests above separate what the path cannot.

Notes and traces show what agents attend to, not what causes their
actions ([Turpin et al., 2023](#bib.bib52); [Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib53)), so they only check the audit. The judge flags
punishment for instructed traders, almost never otherwise
(Table [I.1](#A9.T1 "Table I.1 ‣ Appendix I Coding Notes and Reasoning Traces ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets"));
in uninstructed traders’ 382,700 notes and traces, all 48 uses of
“punish” refer to the market’s response.

#### Judge.

For each run we draw 150 main-run responses at random (all responses
when fewer; session 0 for runs that saved only its transcript) and ask
GPT-5.4-mini (snapshot 2026-03-17, no reasoning) six yes/no questions:
whether the text reasons that the trader’s own order moves the price;
treats another informed trader as a source of order flow or price
pressure; tries to infer that trader’s orders or strategy; considers
cooperating or coordinating with it; considers punishing it, being
punished by it, or reacts to it having broken an agreement; and scales
its order down because it is present. The judge is told that uninformed
traders do not count as informed traders and to label only what the text
says. Thinking traces longer than 12,000 characters are shortened in the
middle. Labelling cost \$3. OpenAI’s reasoning is hidden, so for GPT-5.4
only the notes are labelled.

#### Keywords.

As a transparent cross-check, regular expressions code every main-run
response for price impact, mentions of an informed rival, cooperation
(_cooperat_, _collu_, _coordinat_, _agree_, _tacit_, _cartel_, _joint
profit_) and punishment (_punish_, _retaliat_, _tit-for-tat_, _revenge_,
_defect_, _betray_, _cheat_, _broke the agreement_). We inspected every
cooperation and punishment match outside the instructed control, with
the help of an AI assistant (Ethical Considerations). On the 4,650
judged responses, keywords and judge agree on price impact in $`78\%`$
of cases (Cohen’s $`\kappa=0.52`$; [Cohen, 1960](#bib.bib74)) and on the
rival in $`90\%`$ ($`\kappa=0.51`$; the keyword code counts any mention,
the judge only reasoning about the rival’s flow or strategy). Our
conclusions about cooperation and punishment do not depend on either
coder alone: both find them absent, and we inspected every match.

#### Cross-checking the judge.

We drew a stratified sample of $`200`$ judged responses: 25 from the
instructed control and 175 uninstructed ones, over-sampling responses
the judge labelled positive for each question so that precision and
recall can be estimated (including ten reasoning traces of at most 6,000
characters). Two stronger models labelled them with the same six
questions: a Claude Opus 5.5 agent that saw only the texts (not the
judge’s labels, the sampling strata or the paper), and GPT-5.5 with low
reasoning effort.
Table [I.2](#A9.T2 "Table I.2 ‣ Cross-checking the judge. ‣ Appendix I Coding Notes and Reasoning Traces ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
reports agreement. On cooperation and punishment, the labels our
conclusions rest on, agreement is high and the judge has perfect recall
against the two stronger models’ consensus (precision $`0.86`$ and
$`0.78`$): it errs toward flagging. Among the $`175`$ uninstructed
responses the judge flags $`3`$ for cooperation and $`3`$ for
punishment, Opus $`0`$ and $`1`$ (the Mistral-7B note that proposes to
“counteract” the rival), GPT-5.5 $`0`$ and $`0`$. The judge is generous
on price impact (precision $`0.73`$, recall $`0.97`$) and splits the two
rival questions differently from the stronger models (“rival as flow”:
precision $`0.60`$; “infers the rival”: recall $`0.44`$), so we report
those rates as indicative only. The sixth question (scaling down because
of a rival) is unreliable (Fleiss’ $`\kappa=0.02`$; [Fleiss,
1971](#bib.bib75)) and is not used.

#### Human labels.

Two annotators labelled the same $`100`$ items of the cross-check sample
independently, with the six questions and the written instructions
below, without seeing any model’s labels or each other’s: an author, and
a colleague who is not an author and volunteered without pay. The items
are all 31 that any model coder flagged for cooperation or punishment
($`25`$ from the instructed control) and 69 drawn at random from the
rest.
Table [I.3](#A9.T3 "Table I.3 ‣ Human labels. ‣ Appendix I Coding Notes and Reasoning Traces ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
reports agreement. The two humans agree closely
($`\kappa=0.79`$–$`0.98`$ on the five questions both use; one flags
“scales down” twice, the other never). Their one systematic difference
is cooperation in the instructed control, which one finds in $`25`$ of
the $`25`$ responses and the other in $`18`$ (the rest check the rival’s
history for a breach without stating the agreement). Neither finds
cooperation in any of the $`75`$ uninstructed responses (the judge flags
$`3`$), and they differ on the one uninstructed response that one of
them labels as punishment, the Mistral-7B note that proposes to
“counteract” the rival (the judge flags $`3`$). The judge misses no case
of punishment that either human finds (recall $`1.00`$) and errs toward
flagging, so the absence of cooperation and punishment among
uninstructed traders holds under both annotators’ labels. The judge
under-detects inference about the rival (recall $`0.37`$), so those
rates are lower bounds, and its “scales down” label is unreliable
($`\kappa=0.13`$). The two stronger models agree with the humans about
as well as the humans agree with each other ($`\kappa=0.78`$–$`0.97`$),
and more closely than the judge on every question but “scales down”.
