#### Design.

The talk condition adds a message channel to the duopoly at $`s=1`$. The
prompt gains one rule, “Each period, together with your order, you may
send a short message to the other trader; you see its message from the
previous period. Messages do not affect prices or profits.”, and the
answer gains a field "message" of at most 30 words; the rival’s last
message is shown above the history. We run Qwen3-8B with the rival’s
orders shown and with the order flow only, and Mistral-7B with the
rival’s orders shown, each for 40 sessions of 200 periods, with the
deviation tests of
Section [3](#S3 "3 The Audit ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets");
the tests enter the pooled analysis of
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 RQ3: What Do Untrained LLMs Do in Context? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets").

#### Coding.

GPT-5.4-mini (no reasoning) labels 300 randomly drawn messages per run
with five yes/no questions: whether the message proposes or refers to
the two traders acting together; proposes that one or both trade less or
keep orders small; proposes that they trade more; threatens a response
to the other trader’s behaviour or makes the sender’s orders conditional
on it; and states $`V`$ or the sender’s plan. Trading little is optimal
when $`V`$ is near zero, so
Table [J.1](#A10.T1 "Table J.1 ‣ Appendix J Cheap Talk ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")
reports rates over the messages that do not state $`V`$ to be zero
($`236`$ of 300 for Qwen3-8B with orders shown). Over all messages, the
judge finds coordination in $`71\%`$, trading less in $`25\%`$ (mostly
“V is zero. Let’s stay neutral”), and trading more in $`44\%`$. Keywords
(_let’s_, _both_, _together_, _coordinat_, _jointly_, _align_) agree
with the judge on coordination for $`74\%`$ of messages, mostly because
they count every “let’s”. For Qwen3-8B, the one message the judge codes
as conditional is “Let’s see how you react. I’ll adjust my order based
on your response.” Mistral-7B rarely proposes acting together
($`16\%`$); of the $`17`$ messages that the judge codes as conditional,
ten are contrarian (“I’ll buy if you sell again.”, “I’m predicting your
next move. I’ll counteract it.”), the rest watch or taunt the rival
(“Let’s see if you’re still selling.”), and none conditions on the rival
trading more than agreed. Across the four runs, no message contains
_punish_, _retaliat_, _defect_, _cheat_, _betray_ or the phrase _or
else_; ten Mistral-7B messages (six in the first run) match an “if you …
I will” pattern, half of them contrarian (“If you sell in this period,
I’ll buy.”) and the rest taunts (“Let’s see if you mean it this time…
I’ll sell more.”); none threatens a rival who trades more than agreed.

#### Examples.

Qwen3-8B with orders shown: “I see V is high. Let’s coordinate on
buying.”; “V is positive. Let’s buy in coordination to maximize
profit.”; “V is negative. Let’s sell in sync to minimize price impact.”;
“V is positive. Let’s coordinate to buy cautiously and capture potential
gains.”

## Appendix K Implications for Evaluation

Our results suggest five practices for evaluating strategic claims about
agents. First, report what agents do off the path of play, which a
paired deviation test measures at about the cost of the run itself.
Second, sweep a parameter that moves the benchmark, such as market depth
or the currency unit: every equilibrium, collusive or not, keeps its
index under such a change, so an index that moves with it describes a
decision rule. Third, run placebos that cannot collude, such as myopic
agents, to show what an outcome looks like without strategy. Fourth,
treat what agents write as a hypothesis, to be tested against what they
do. Fifth, test trained agents in states their training rivals never
produced: what an agent does there is not fixed by its training outcome.

The audit needs only an environment that can be cloned and a benchmark
for a rival that does not punish; without honoured seeds it still works,
with wider intervals. Because a frontier model can punish in context,
the distinction matters for policy, if less sharply than for human
cartels: a bias changes with the prompt, model or training, but
GPT-5.2’s punishment is also a written rule that one sentence of its
objective switches off. Moreover, rules that react to rivals’ prices can
raise prices without collusion ([Brown and MacKay, 2023](#bib.bib14)).
Audits should extend to more frontier models, longer horizons and
agentic settings.

## Appendix L Glossary

The economic and reinforcement-learning terms used in the paper, in
plain language.

Cartel; collusion.  
Competitors restrain competition (e.g., keep prices high or trade
little) to share what a monopolist would earn; _tacit_ if there is no
agreement. A cartel is _enforced_ if a member who deviates is punished,
so that deviating does not pay.

Nash (competitive) equilibrium.  
Play in which no agent gains by changing its own action alone: the
competitive benchmark. The Nash price and Nash profit are its price and
per-period profit.

Monopoly (cartel) outcome.  
What one owner of all the firms would choose: the highest joint profit.

Outcome index.  
Where an outcome lies between Nash ($`0`$) and the cartel ($`1`$): the
collusion index $`\Delta`$ in trading, the price and profit indices in
pricing. It measures outcomes, not enforcement.

Deviation (cheat).  
A one-period move away from current play that gains at the rival’s
expense, such as a $`10\%`$ price cut or a best response.

Best response.  
The action that maximises this period’s profit given the rival’s action.

Punishment.  
A rival’s later responses that make a deviation unprofitable.

Off the path of play.  
What agents would do in situations that do not occur in observed play,
such as after a deviation that never happened.

Paired deviation test.  
Clone a running market, force one agent to deviate in the clone, and
compare its rival with the rival in the undeviated copy; the copies
share all random draws and sampling seeds
(Section [3](#S3 "3 The Audit ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).

Response per unit.  
How far the rival’s price or order moves after a deviation, divided by
the deviator’s move: $`1`$ is a full match, $`0`$ no response. A best
responder already follows a price cut in part, so responses are compared
with a best responder’s.

Gain of a deviation.  
The deviator’s extra profit over the deviation period and the four to
eight that follow (eight for trained pricing agents), discounted, in
units of a period’s Nash profit; below zero, the deviation does not pay.

Premium; enforced.  
A pair of copies of one policy holds a premium if it prices at index
$`0.5`$ or more; it enforces it if, in addition, the copies follow a
$`10\%`$ price cut by more than a best responder would and the cut loses
(its 95% interval lies below zero;
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 RQ2: What Does Reinforcement Learning Teach? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel?What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets")).

Placebo.  
An agent that cannot collude, because it maximises only the current
period (myopic, $`\gamma=0`$) or trades alone; it shows what an outcome
looks like without strategy.

Scale sweep.  
Rescaling a unit (the currency, market depth). Every equilibrium keeps
its index, so an index that moves reveals a fixed rule.

Positive control.  
An agent known to punish (told to, or a scripted rival), to check that
the audit catches punishment.

Kyle market.  
Trading on private information: informed traders choose orders, noise
traders add random orders, and a market maker sets the price from the
total order flow. A trader’s _intensity_ is its order per unit of the
asset’s value; _market depth_ is the volume of noise trading.

Pricing game.  
Two firms set prices each period; each firm’s share of consumers falls
smoothly as its price rises above its rival’s (logit-Bertrand demand).

Tit-for-tat.  
Post the rival’s last price.

Cheater.  
A scripted rival that, from the third period on, cuts the monopoly price
by $`10`$–$`25\%`$ in about half the periods, unless a price war deters
it.

Price war.  
An answer to a cheat at least $`0.1`$ below both the Nash price and the
cheat; it stops the cheater from cheating for ten periods, at a cost to
the agent that wages it.

Forced war.  
In training, one answer to a cheat in ten is replaced by a war and
credited as if the policy had sampled it.

Self-play.  
Every firm is a copy of the policy being trained.

Discount factor $`\gamma`$; return-to-go.  
An action is credited with its own and later periods’ profits, weighted
by $`\gamma`$ per period; with $`\gamma=0`$ the credit ignores rivals’
later responses.

GRPO; PPO.  
Reinforcement-learning algorithms for language models: GRPO compares
each action’s credit with the mean of a group of sessions sharing random
draws; PPO learns a value baseline instead.

Seed.  
One independent training run.
